title: Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS(0))
subtitle: How DNS grew past its 512-byte limit without breaking the servers that never heard of it.
summary: EDNS(0) lets a DNS message carry a special OPT pseudo-record in its additional section. With it, a requestor can announce how large a UDP reply it can accept, set extra flags such as DO (DNSSEC OK), use a 12-bit response code, and attach optional {code, value} options. The original 1987 format could do none of this. RFC 6891 replaces RFC 2671 and makes OPT support mandatory.

eli5.summary: Old phone books only had room for a few lines per person. EDNS(0) is a sticky note on the question that says "I have a big enough page to read a long answer, and here are some other things I can handle."

questions: why is the dns udp limit 512 bytes
what is the dns opt record
what does the do bit mean in dns
what udp buffer size should dns use
why do dns queries fall back to tcp

tldr.problem: Plain DNS limits UDP messages to 512 bytes and has no room for new flags, response codes or capability announcements.
tldr.mechanism: A requestor adds one OPT pseudo-record (RR type 41) to the additional section. Its CLASS field holds the UDP payload size, its TTL field holds the extended RCODE, version and flags, and its RDATA holds options.
tldr.outcome: Larger UDP answers, DNSSEC signalling and a registry of options work through one hop-by-hop mechanism, and old servers fall back cleanly to plain DNS.

today: EDNS(0) is everywhere in DNS. Resolvers and authoritative servers send OPT records on most queries, and DNSSEC validation depends on the DO bit it carries. Later specifications add options through the IANA EDNS option registry, for example DNS cookies and EDNS Client Subnet. Tools such as dig show the OPT record in an "OPT PSEUDOSECTION". In practice, operators often choose UDP sizes well below 4096 to avoid IP fragmentation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Domain Name System in RFC 1035 fixed its message layout in 1987. Over UDP a message could be at most 512 bytes, the header flags and response codes were nearly used up, and there was no way for one side to tell the other what it could do. Adding IPv6 addresses or DNSSEC signatures made that squeeze worse.

RFC 6891 describes the extension mechanism known as EDNS(0), first specified in RFC 2671 by one of the same authors. It refines that text using deployment experience, obsoletes RFC 2671, and also obsoletes RFC 2673 (Binary Labels). EDNS is hop-by-hop: the stub resolver and the recursive resolver agree on it between themselves, and the recursive resolver and an authoritative server agree separately.

The "(0)" is the EDNS version number. Version 0 is the only version this document defines.
sections.eli5: Old DNS notes were written on tiny cards. This document is the rule for stapling one extra card to a note so it can say more, without confusing people who only read the first card.

sections.title: Why plain DNS ran out of room
sections.content:
The RFC names three limits. First, a UDP message could not exceed 512 octets without the extension, and larger content such as several IPv6 addresses or DNSSEC data such as RRSIG and DNSKEY records often did not fit. A server then had to set the TC (truncated) bit and make the client retry over TCP. Second, the 4-bit RCODE and the few unused header flags were close to exhausted. Third, RFC 1035 gave no way for a client to advertise its capabilities.

The EDNS(0) answer is to spend one extra record. That record lets UDP carry bigger answers, which the RFC says helps scalability by avoiding widespread use of TCP, and it supplies extra flag and RCODE space.

The RFC also says to avoid adding new RCODEs where possible and to use a flag only when needed for resolution to work. For many uses, a new option code is the preferred route.
sections.eli5: A short letter fits in a small envelope. A letter with photos does not. The sender needs a way to say "I have a bigger mailbox, send the whole thing" so nobody has to make a second trip.

sections.title: The OPT pseudo-record
sections.content:
An OPT record has RR type 41 and goes in the additional section of a message. It is called a pseudo-RR because it carries no DNS data. It holds only control information for one question-and-answer exchange, and it MUST NOT be cached, forwarded, or stored in or loaded from master files.

A message may contain at most one OPT record. If a query arrives with more than one, the responder MUST return FORMERR (RCODE 1). If a request has an OPT record, a compliant responder MUST include one in its response. Where TSIG or SIG(0) records are present they still have to come last in the additional section.

CLASS field
Reused to carry the sender's UDP payload size.
TTL field
Reused for the extended RCODE, the VERSION and the flags.
RDATA
Holds zero or more options as code, length and data.
sections.eli5: The OPT record is a sticky note that looks like a normal record but is really a message to the other side. It is read once and then thrown away, never filed in the cabinet.

sections.title: Wire format
sections.content:
The fixed part of an OPT RR is the usual resource-record layout with new meanings. NAME MUST be 0, the root domain, a single zero octet. TYPE is 41. CLASS is the requestor's UDP payload size. TTL is split into four pieces. RDLEN gives the length of the RDATA.

The 32-bit TTL holds EXTENDED-RCODE (8 bits), VERSION (8 bits), the DO flag (1 bit) and Z (15 bits). EXTENDED-RCODE supplies the upper 8 bits of a 12-bit response code, joined with the 4 bits in the DNS header, and a value of 0 means the plain 4-bit RCODE is in use. DO is the DNSSEC OK bit from RFC 3225. Senders set Z to zero and receivers ignore it.

Each option inside RDATA is OPTION-CODE (16 bits), OPTION-LENGTH (16 bits, the size of the data in octets) and OPTION-DATA. The order of options is not defined, and any option code a receiver does not understand MUST be ignored.

VERSION tells the other side the sender's implementation level. If a responder does not implement the requested version it MUST answer with RCODE BADVERS, and its reply still states its own highest version.
sections.eli5: The note has a few boxes to tick: how big a page I can read, whether I want the security stamps, and a spot for extra requests. Anything on the note you do not recognise, you simply skip.

sections.title: Choosing a UDP payload size
sections.content:
The requestor's UDP payload size is the largest UDP payload it can reassemble and deliver in its network stack. Values below 512 MUST be treated as 512. The requestor should advertise something it can actually receive: behind a firewall that blocks fragments, a size that forces fragmentation will stop large replies from arriving at all. The advertised size MUST NOT be cached for use beyond the transaction it was sent in.

The RFC does not recommend advertising an architectural limit such as 64 KB. It suggests 4096 octets as a reasonable starting point and a fallback ladder: try a large size such as 4096, then somewhere between 1280 and 1410 bytes, which has a good chance of fitting in a single Ethernet frame, and finally 512 if needed, accepting that big answers will then cause a TCP retry.

Very large values guarantee IP fragmentation, and losing one fragment loses the whole answer. Values that are too small push traffic back to TCP, which the RFC notes is especially costly with DNSSEC.
sections.eli5: If you ask for a giant parcel, it may arrive in pieces and one piece can get lost. If you ask for tiny parcels you will make lots of extra trips. The best choice is a size that comfortably fits through the door.

sections.title: Negotiation, fallback and middleboxes
sections.content:
The presence of an OPT record in a request means the requestor fully implements that EDNS version. Its absence MUST be read as no EDNS support, and the responder MUST NOT put an OPT record in its reply. A responder that does not implement EDNS MUST answer FORMERR to a message containing OPT and MUST NOT include OPT in the response. If the OPT record itself is malformed, the responder returns FORMERR but includes an OPT record, so the requestor can tell the two cases apart.

A requestor that finds EDNS unsupported MAY retry without OPT and MAY remember that briefly. It should not fall back if it needs DNSSEC or another EDNS-only feature. Even a truncated reply must at minimum contain the header, the question section and an OPT record.

Middleboxes such as firewalls and load balancers MUST NOT limit UDP DNS messages to 512 bytes. Ones that merely forward to a recursive resolver MUST NOT modify or delete the OPT contents. Smarter ones that answer queries should process OPT and treat incoming and outgoing requests as separate transactions.

Section 6.2.6 points to RFC 5625 for DNS proxy guidance.
sections.eli5: If you hand the note to someone who cannot read it, they say "I don't understand" and you can try again with a plain question. The people in between just have to pass the note along without scribbling on it.

sections.title: Extended labels and registries
sections.content:
RFC 2671 also reserved the label type with bit pattern 01 in the first two bits of a label's first octet (values 64 to 127) for extended label types. Only one was ever proposed, the Binary Label in RFC 2673, and extended labels proved extremely hard to deploy. RFC 6891 obsoletes RFC 2673 and deprecates Binary Labels, saying implementations MUST NOT generate or pass them, and that new extended labels should be considered only after careful evaluation.

IANA assigned RR type 41 to OPT, assigned EDNS extended RCODE 16 to BADVERS, and reserved option code 65535 for future expansion. At publication, option codes 0 to 4 were assigned, 5 to 65000 were unassigned, and 65001 to 65534 were for local or experimental use. New option codes are assigned by Expert Review, new EDNS(0) flags need IETF Standards Action, as do new entries in the EDNS Version Number registry, and a new RCODE needs IETF Review.

The registry has grown well beyond what the RFC lists. Consult the IANA "DNS EDNS0 Option Codes" registry for the current list.
sections.eli5: There is a list of allowed note-types kept by a librarian. Adding a new kind of tick box is hard and needs a big meeting, while adding a new kind of extra request only needs a quick check.

sections.title: Security considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's security section is short and about size. A requestor that advertises a large buffer might let an attacker make responders send messages too big for intermediate gateways to forward, which could lead to ICMP storms between gateways and responders. Announcing very large sizes may also cause middleboxes to drop DNS messages, which causes retransmissions with no hope of success, and some devices have been found to reject fragmented UDP packets.

The opposite error costs too. Announcing sizes that are too small causes fallback to TCP and extra load on DNS servers, which matters most with DNSSEC because the answers are much larger.

Size choice is a trade-off the RFC leaves to implementers and administrators, not a single correct number.
sections.eli5: Asking for a huge parcel can make the mail carrier's truck jam up the road, and asking for tiny ones keeps the post office busy. Pick a middle size.

fields.name: NAME
fields.desc: MUST be 0, the root domain (one zero octet).

fields.name: CLASS (UDP payload size)
fields.desc: Requestor's UDP payload size in octets; values below 512 are treated as 512.

fields.name: EXTENDED-RCODE
fields.desc: Upper 8 bits of the 12-bit RCODE; 0 means an unextended RCODE.

fields.name: VERSION
fields.desc: Implementation level of the sender; 0 is full conformance with RFC 6891.

fields.name: Z
fields.desc: Set to zero by senders, ignored by receivers.

fields.name: RDLEN
fields.desc: Length in octets of all RDATA (the options).

fields.name: OPTION-CODE
fields.desc: Assigned by Expert Review; unknown codes MUST be ignored.

fields.name: OPTION-LENGTH
fields.desc: Size in octets of OPTION-DATA, which follows.

messages.label: Query + OPT (size 4096, DO)
messages.note: Requestor advertises its UDP payload size and flags.

messages.label: Response + OPT
messages.note: Responder MUST include an OPT record; its VERSION shows its highest level.

messages.label: Query + OPT
messages.note: Sent to a server that predates EDNS.

messages.label: FORMERR, no OPT
messages.note: Unextended responders answer FORMERR and omit OPT.

messages.label: Query without OPT
messages.note: The requestor MAY fall back and remember it briefly, unless it needs DNSSEC.

data.title: dig +dnssec (OPT pseudosection, illustrative)
data.code:
;; OPT PSEUDOSECTION:
; EDNS: version: 0, flags: do; udp: 1232
